summary.text: Write the summand as \(t_j(n)=\binom nj n^{\overline j}\).  Shifting \(n\) by \(k\) leaves the rising factorial unchanged modulo \(k\), while \(n^{\overline j}=j!\binom{n+j-1}{j}\) converts the remaining factor \(\binom{n+k}{j}j!\) into a falling factorial, also unchanged modulo \(k\); thus corresponding summands are congruent, and extending the shorter sum introduces only zero terms because \(\binom nj=0\) for \(j>n\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=n!\,[x^n]\frac{e^x}{(1-x)^n}\qquad(n\geq 0).
\]
We prove that for all nonnegative integers \(n\) and \(d\),
\[
a(n+d)\equiv a(n)\pmod d.
\]

We begin by putting the coefficient formula into a finite-sum form suited to congruences.

For nonnegative integers \(m,j\), define
\[
B(m,j)=\binom{m+j-1}{j},
\]
with the natural exceptional convention \(B(0,0)=1\). Thus, when \(m=0\) and \(j>0\), we have \(B(0,j)=\binom{j-1}{j}=0\). Equivalently, these are the coefficients in
\[
(1-x)^{-m}=\sum_{j\geq 0}B(m,j)x^j.
\]
For \(m\geq1\), this is the usual negative-binomial expansion
\[
(1-x)^{-m}=\sum_{j\geq0}\binom{m+j-1}{j}x^j;
\]
for \(m=0\), it simply says that \((1-x)^0=1\).

Since
\[
e^x=\sum_{i\geq0}\frac{x^i}{i!},
\]
the coefficient of \(x^m\) in their product is
\[
[x^m]\frac{e^x}{(1-x)^m}
 =\sum_{j=0}^m \frac{1}{(m-j)!}B(m,j).
\]
Multiplying by \(m!\) gives
\[
a(m)=\sum_{j=0}^m \frac{m!}{(m-j)!}B(m,j).
\]
The elementary identity
\[
\frac{m!}{(m-j)!}=\binom mj j!\qquad(0\leq j\leq m)
\]
therefore yields
\[
a(m)=\sum_{j=0}^m T(m,j),
\qquad
T(m,j):=\binom mj B(m,j)j!.
\tag{1}
\]
This also covers \(m=0\): the sole term is \(T(0,0)=1\). We use the standard convention \(\binom mj=0\) for \(j>m\), so \(T(m,j)=0\) whenever \(j>m\).

We next introduce rising and falling factorials. Write
\[
m^{\overline j}=m(m+1)\cdots(m+j-1),
\qquad
m^{\underline j}=m(m-1)\cdots(m-j+1),
\]
where an empty product is \(1\). For falling factorials of nonnegative integers, if \(j>m\), the product contains a zero factor and hence is zero. The standard product identities are
\[
m^{\overline j}=j!B(m,j),
\qquad
m^{\underline j}=j!\binom mj.
\tag{2}
\]
For example, when \(m\geq1\), the first identity follows from
\[
m^{\overline j}=\frac{(m+j-1)!}{(m-1)!}
 =j!\binom{m+j-1}{j},
\]
and the cases involving \(m=0\) follow directly: both sides equal \(1\) when \(j=0\), and both sides equal \(0\) when \(j>0\). The second identity follows from
\[
m^{\underline j}=\frac{m!}{(m-j)!}=j!\binom mj
\]
when \(j\leq m\), while both sides vanish when \(j>m\).

By the first identity in (2), the summand in (1) can be written as
\[
T(m,j)=\binom mj\,m^{\overline j}.
\tag{3}
\]

We now establish two elementary periodicity facts for factorial products. Fix nonnegative integers \(n,d,j\).

First,
\[
(n+d)^{\overline j}\equiv n^{\overline j}\pmod d.
\tag{4}
\]
Indeed, the corresponding factors are congruent:
\[
n+d+r\equiv n+r\pmod d
\]
for every \(r\). Multiplying these congruences for \(r=0,1,\ldots,j-1\) proves (4). Equivalently, one may prove it by induction on \(j\), using
\[
m^{\overline{j+1}}=(m+j)m^{\overline j}.
\]

Second,
\[
(n+d)^{\underline j}\equiv n^{\underline j}\pmod d.
\tag{5}
\]
There is a small boundary issue here because the falling products may reach zero, so we give a complete induction proof. For \(j=0\), both sides are \(1\). Suppose (5) is known for \(j\). Recall the recurrence, valid for nonnegative integers with truncated subtraction,
\[
m^{\underline{j+1}}=(m-j)m^{\underline j}.
\]
If \(j\leq n\), then
\[
n+d-j=(n-j)+d\equiv n-j\pmod d.
\]
Together with the induction hypothesis, multiplication gives
\[
(n+d)^{\underline{j+1}}
 =(n+d-j)(n+d)^{\underline j}
 \equiv(n-j)n^{\underline j}
 =n^{\underline{j+1}}\pmod d.
\]
If instead \(n<j\), then \(n^{\underline j}=0\), because the falling product has already passed through a zero factor. The induction hypothesis consequently says
\[
(n+d)^{\underline j}\equiv0\pmod d.
\]
Multiplying by the additional factor \(n+d-j\) shows that \((n+d)^{\underline{j+1}}\) is also divisible by \(d\). Meanwhile \(n^{\underline{j+1}}=0\). Thus the desired congruence holds in this case as well, completing the induction and proving (5).

The key step is now to prove, for every summation index \(j\),
\[
T(n+d,j)\equiv T(n,j)\pmod d.
\tag{6}
\]
Using (3) and then the rising-factorial congruence (4), we first have
\[
T(n+d,j)
 =\binom{n+d}{j}(n+d)^{\overline j}
 \equiv \binom{n+d}{j}n^{\overline j}\pmod d.
\tag{7}
\]
It would not in general be valid simply to replace \(\binom{n+d}{j}\) by \(\binom nj\), because binomial coefficients themselves need not have period \(d\) in their upper argument modulo \(d\). The extra rising-factorial factor supplies exactly what is needed.

By (2),
\[
n^{\overline j}=j!B(n,j).
\]
Therefore the expression on the right side of (7) can be regrouped as
\[
\binom{n+d}{j}n^{\overline j}
 =\left(j!\binom{n+d}{j}\right)B(n,j)
 =(n+d)^{\underline j}B(n,j).
\]
Applying the falling-factorial congruence (5) and multiplying by the fixed integer \(B(n,j)\), we obtain
\[
(n+d)^{\underline j}B(n,j)
 \equiv n^{\underline j}B(n,j)\pmod d.
\]
Using (2) once more, the last expression is
\[
n^{\underline j}B(n,j)
 =\left(j!\binom nj\right)B(n,j)
 =\binom nj\,n^{\overline j}
 =T(n,j).
\]
Combined with (7), this proves the termwise congruence (6).

We can now compare the two finite sums. If \(d=0\), then \(n+d=n\), so the claimed statement is simply the equality \(a(n)=a(n)\). Assume henceforth that \(d>0\).

By (1),
\[
a(n+d)=\sum_{j=0}^{n+d}T(n+d,j).
\]
Also,
\[
a(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}T(n,j).
\]
Because \(\binom nj=0\) whenever \(j>n\), all the additional terms \(T(n,j)\) with \(n<j\leq n+d\) vanish. Hence we may extend the latter sum to the same range:
\[
a(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n+d}T(n,j).
\]
For every \(j\) in this common range, (6) gives
\[
T(n+d,j)\equiv T(n,j)\pmod d.
\]
Congruences are preserved under finite addition, so summing these termwise congruences gives
\[
a(n+d)=\sum_{j=0}^{n+d}T(n+d,j)
\equiv\sum_{j=0}^{n+d}T(n,j)=a(n)\pmod d.
\]
Thus, for all nonnegative integers \(n\) and \(d\),
\[
\boxed{a(n+d)\equiv a(n)\pmod d}.
\]
